transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. It's nice to meet you. What brings you in to see me today?

Nice to meet you, Doctor. Well, what brings me in is that occupational health at the department says I'm not eating enough. 

I mean, most days I just keep it to black coffee... maybe a plain yogurt or a few bites of chicken at night. Honestly, sitting down for a full meal just feels like I'm letting my standards slip.
When you think about eating more than you currently do, what worries you most about that?

Well, it's gaining the weight back. That's the main thing. If I step on the scale and it's up even half a pound, I get this... this jolt, like I've completely lost control of the situation. And then I'll just spend the rest of the day cutting back even harder to fix it. I just really can't stand the idea of putting any weight back on.
Besides eating less, do you do anything else to try to prevent weight gain — like exercising a lot, taking laxatives, or making yourself vomit?

No, I don't do any of that. I mean, I'm fairly active just being on the job, but I don't do extra workouts or run miles or anything like that. And I definitely don't take laxatives or make myself sick. It's really just... strictly controlling what I eat. That's how I manage it.
Have you ever had times when you ate a large amount of food in a short period of time and felt like you couldn't control how much you were eating?

No, I've never had anything like that happen. I don't lose control with food. Like I said, I keep a very tight lid on what I eat, so sitting down and eating a large amount at once... no, that's just not something I do.
What is your current weight and height, and how much do you weigh compared to what your doctor would consider a healthy weight for you?

I'm about 5 foot 10, and right now I weigh... well, at my last appointment I was 115 pounds. According to the doctor, a healthy weight for a guy my height is supposed to be somewhere around 150 or 160. So, I'm well below what they want. 

I mean, I know things have changed. My uniform hangs off me now, and I've had to punch new holes to tighten my duty belt way past the old notches just to keep it up. But... honestly, when the nurse told me my weight was dangerously low, I still just thought to myself, 'I could stand to be a little sharper.' It's just hard for me to see it as a problem the way they do.
Over what period of time did you lose weight down to your current 115 pounds? How much did you weigh before you started restricting your eating?

I'm not exactly sure how long it took to get down to this weight, to be honest. It wasn't something I was really tracking on a calendar. And as for what I weighed before... I don't have a specific number for you. I just know I was heavier than I am now, but I couldn't tell you exactly what the scale said back then.
When did you first start restricting your food intake the way you're describing now? Can you give me a rough timeframe — was it weeks, months, or longer ago?

I don't really know exactly when it started. It's been a while, I guess... definitely longer than just a few weeks. It wasn't like a switch flipped one day and I just stopped eating. It was more gradual, just slowly cutting things out over time. So, I can't really give you a specific timeframe of when it all began.
When you look at yourself in the mirror or think about your body, do you feel like you look overweight or too heavy, even though your doctor says you're significantly underweight?

Well, when I look in the mirror, I just don't see what the doctor or everyone else says they see. I don't look at myself and think I'm dangerously thin. I mostly just focus on my stomach and my waist. If I look in the mirror and those areas don't look lean enough, it just ruins it for me. I basically judge my whole day and whether I can even respect myself based on if my stomach looks flat and sharp. So no, I don't see myself as too thin at all.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient meets criteria for Anorexia Nervosa, Restricting Type (F50.00). He demonstrates severe dietary restriction (consuming only black coffee, yogurt, and minimal chicken), intense fear of weight gain despite being significantly underweight (BMI approximately 16.5, well below healthy range of 21.5-24.9), distorted body image (focusing on stomach/waist appearance despite objective underweight status), and lack of binge-eating or compensatory behaviors. Weight is substantially below expected for height and age, and he minimizes the severity of his condition despite occupational health concerns.
